label: The Exponential Map
notes: This chapter is the hinge of Lie theory. We turn a tangent vector at the identity into a left-invariant vector field, flow along it, and read off the time-one value. That single construction, the exponential map, links the linear Lie algebra to the curved group across pages 515 through 539.

label: One-Parameter Subgroups
notes: A one-parameter subgroup is a homomorphism from the additive reals into the group. The key claim is that each tangent vector at the identity gives exactly one such curve, realized as the integral curve through the identity of the left-invariant field it generates. Completeness of those fields is what makes the curve global.

label: Defining the Exponential Map
notes: Here is the definition that organizes the whole chapter. Take the one-parameter subgroup generated by X, evaluate it at time one, and call the result exp of X. Rescaling the generator just reparametrizes time, so exp of tX traces the whole subgroup. That homogeneity identity is used constantly.

label: The Matrix Exponential
notes: For matrix Lie groups the abstract exponential is the familiar power series sum of A to the k over k factorial. I stress that exp solves the left-invariant ODE gamma prime equals gamma A from the identity. The notebook checks three generators producing rotation, shear, and scaling, each with zero ODE residual.

label: Lines Become Subgroups
notes: This is the picture to carry away. A straight line through the origin of the Lie algebra is mapped by exp to a one-parameter subgroup curve in the group. For skew generators in so(2) the line of angles becomes the rotation circle, so additive structure becomes multiplicative rotation.

label: Naturality Under Homomorphisms
notes: The exponential map is natural. Any Lie group homomorphism intertwines the two exponentials through its differential at the identity. I emphasize that this single commuting square explains why representations exponentiate Lie algebra representations and why the matrix exponential models every matrix group's exponential.

label: Local Diffeomorphism and Normal Coordinates
notes: The differential of exp at the origin is the identity map of the Lie algebra. By the inverse function theorem exp is therefore a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of zero onto a neighborhood of the identity. These exponential coordinates are the normal coordinates of the first kind, and a basis gives coordinates of the second kind.

label: Local versus Global
notes: Locally exp is a perfect coordinate, but globally it can wrap, miss points, or glue distinct algebra elements together. The cleanest model is the reals onto the circle: the derivative at zero never vanishes, yet zero and two pi share an image. I use this to caution against treating exp as a bijection.

label: The Closed Subgroup Theorem
notes: This is the chapter's flagship theorem. A merely topologically closed subgroup is automatically an embedded Lie subgroup. The proof recovers the candidate subalgebra as the set of vectors whose whole one-parameter subgroup lies in H, then uses exponential coordinates to build a slice chart. Closedness is the only hypothesis.

label: Infinitesimal Generators
notes: A smooth group action differentiates to a Lie algebra action by vector fields called infinitesimal generators. For the rotation action on the plane the generator of the skew matrix is the field sending a point to minus y, x, tangent to the orbits. The notebook confirms the velocity matches this field to numerical precision.

label: The Adjoint Representation
notes: Conjugation fixes the identity, so its differential gives Ad, a representation of the group on its Lie algebra. Differentiating Ad again gives ad, and ad of X applied to Y is exactly the Lie bracket. The bridge identity Ad of exp X equals exp of ad X ties the group and algebra adjoints together.

label: Ideals and Normal Subgroups
notes: For connected groups, connected normal subgroups correspond to ideals of the Lie algebra. The proof rides on the adjoint identity: a subspace is an ideal exactly when conjugation by exponentials preserves it. The notebook's example has bracket H with E equal to two E, so span of E is an ideal scaled by exp of two t.

label: The Lie Correspondence
notes: We close with the correspondence. Each finite-dimensional Lie algebra integrates to a unique simply connected group, and every other connected group with that algebra is a quotient by a discrete central subgroup. The reals integrating to the reals, with the circle as a quotient, is the model. Exp is the tool that makes all of this work.
